deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is a sequence of aphorisms and methodological remarks, continuing the previous page's reflections on axiomatics, the absence of an 'ignorabimus', and the claim that most theorems are still undiscovered. Paraphrased in order:

(1) End of a sentence from the previous page about the axiomatic method: it also gives 'the best footholds for memory'.

(2) To compare two lecturers (Docenten) as teachers, what matters is what each one lectures on: whether he takes on the difficult scientific questions or is merely a crammer ('Einpauker').

(3) Special results that are merely interesting, striking or unexpected are often the beginnings of more general, larger theories. ('bloss' is added above the line.)

(4) One must always keep in mind that most theorems in mathematics are still undiscovered. This repeats the remark on the previous page.

(5) The understanding is like the eye. The eye sees sharply only at one very small spot (the fovea, written here as 'Sehfleck' or similar) and covers the rest by rapid movement. Likewise the understanding must have its sharpness at one place and handle everything else through practised mobility. 'Beweglichkeit' is underlined.

(6) On Kronecker's general views: truth is supposed to lie mostly in the middle, but here it lies entirely on one side, namely the side opposite Kronecker. This is a jab at Kronecker's finitist and constructivist programme.

(7) 'Less is so often more.' It is always a fault of a paper when the author writes into it everything he knew. Kronecker, however, committed a still worse fault by writing in more than he knew. This alludes to Kronecker's unproved or incompletely justified claims.

There is nothing mathematical to reconstruct. The page documents Hilbert's methodological and polemical views, around the period of his axiomatic work and the Frege correspondence (c. 1899–1900; the next page quotes his postcard to Frege).

deep.surprise_reason: These are non-mathematical aphorisms from Hilbert's notebooks. The optimism about undiscovered theorems and the hostility to Kronecker are well documented Hilbert attitudes, and similar notebook remarks have been quoted by historians such as Rowe, Corry and Sieg. The specific Kronecker witticism and the eye analogy are pleasant details but not historically significant.
